Disperse

/dih-SPURS/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Disperse means to scatter in different directions, or to cause a crowd or group to break up and spread out.

By noon the storm clouds had begun to disperse, leaving patches of clear blue sky.

Worked Example

A single gust of wind hit the dandelion, and hundreds of seeds dispersed across the meadow. Within a minute they had drifted so far apart that no two seeds landed anywhere near each other.

The seeds start as one tight cluster and end up scattered in every direction across a wide area, which is precisely the physical spreading-apart that disperse describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scatter: the quick, everyday word for people or things darting off in all directions; disperse is the formal term for a group breaking up

spread: to extend over a wider area

disband: to break up a group so members go separate ways

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

gather: to come together in one place

assemble: to collect into an organized group

Where it sits · how fully the group breaks apart — spread → disperse → flee

spread vs. disperse: Spread simply means to cover more area, while disperse means the group actually breaks apart into separate pieces moving different ways.

flee vs. disperse: Disperse is calmer than flee, which adds panic and urgent escape to the scattering.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: apart, in different directions (not negation here)

Root — sperse

Root — sperse: to scatter, sprinkle (Latin spargere, sparsus)

Put it together

Put it together: Heads up: in this word dis- means 'apart, in different directions,' not the 'not, opposite of' sense this unit is named for. Disperse comes from dis- (apart) plus Latin spargere (to scatter, to sprinkle), so it literally means 'to scatter apart.'

Use the root in a new word: sparse

Use the root in a new word: sparse: Trees were sparse on the rocky hillside, scattered so thinly that you could count them from the road.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral, slightly formal

Disperse describes a group or collection physically breaking apart and moving in different directions, and it is the standard verb for crowds. Unlike dissipate, which describes something fading away gradually, or dispel, which describes deliberately eliminating a feeling or belief, disperse specifically describes a group or crowd physically scattering in different directions.
